idiom_name: make(chan Job, N) buffered channel + a fixed set of worker goroutines
implementation_notes: The buffered channel is the queue and its capacity is the bound: send blocks once the buffer holds N values, so a burst is stored and the producers are paced instead of rejected - the structure the Go pipelines article calls a stage pipeline with buffered channels. A worker is a goroutine doing for job := range jobs, and fan-out is simply several goroutines ranging over the same channel; the channel replaces any hand-written queue, mutex or condition variable. The classic structure is only justified when it must survive restarts or span hosts: then keep the same producer/consumer shape but put a broker client (or a durable log) in place of the channel, because a channel's buffer is in-memory and lost with the process. Use select with a default branch, or a semaphore-style token channel, when a reject or shed path is wanted instead of a blocking send.
pitfalls: An unbounded design is a channel with a huge capacity (or a slice plus mutex): it moves the failure to memory exhaustion instead of bounding the burst.
Goroutines leak whenever a consumer stops receiving while producers keep sending; cancellation must be plumbed through a done channel or context, as the pipelines article shows.
Sending on a closed channel panics and closing from the consumer side breaks the multi-producer case - the producer side closes, and only after all sends are done.
A channel capacity is not a rate limit: it bounds the burst, not requests per second to the dependency.
